'''James Daniel''' "'''BJ'''" '''Bjorken''' (June 22, 1934 – August 6, 2024) was an American [[theoretical physicist]]. He was a [[Putnam Fellow]] in 1954,<ref name="MMA">{{cite web |title=Putnam Competition Individual and Team Winners |url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]] |access-date=December 10, 2021 |archive-date=March 12, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140312205244/http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/putnam-competition-individual-and-team-winners |url-status=dead }}</ref> received a BS in physics from [[MIT]] in 1956, and obtained his PhD from [[Stanford University]] in 1959. Bjorken was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in the fall of 1962.<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/ Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars]</ref> He was also emeritus professor in the [[SLAC Theory Group]] at the [[Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]], and was a member of the Theory Department of the [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]] (1979–1989).

Bjorken was awarded the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|Dirac Medal of the ICTP]] in 2004;  and, in 2015, the [[Wolf Prize in Physics]]  and the [[European Physical Society|EPS]] [[High Energy and Particle Physics Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://eps-hepp.web.cern.ch/hepp-prize-awards.php|title=High Energy Particle Physics Prize|access-date=February 7, 2026|archive-date=|archive-url=|url-status=|last=High Energy Particle Physics Division of EPS}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
James Bjorken's father, J. Daniel Bjorken, was an immigrant from Sweden near [[Lake Siljan]]. He changed his surname from "Björkén" to Bjorken upon arriving in the US; he moved to Chicago to work as an electrical engineer, which was where he met his future wife, Edith. James Bjorken grew up in Chicago and enjoyed mathematics, chemistry, the French horn, and watching the [[Chicago Cubs]] play at [[Wrigley Field]]. After graduating from [[Maine East High School]] in 1952, he decided to attend [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) over the [[University of Chicago]]. Despite being offered more financial aid to attend the University of Chicago, his parents advised him that he should move further away to find his independence.<ref name="Bjorken">{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev-nucl-101918-023359|doi-access=free|title="Why do We do Physics? Because Physics is Fun!"|year=2020|last1=Bjorken|first1=James D.|journal=Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science|volume=70|pages=1–20|bibcode=2020ARNPS..70....1B}}</ref>

At MIT, he quickly decided to major in physics; one of the main reasons was his enjoyment of the lectures that [[Hans Mueller (physicist)|Hans Mueller]] gave. Another of his influences at MIT was [[Sidney Drell]], who became his mentor. After graduating in 1956, he attended [[Stanford University]], graduating with his PhD in 1959 and staying on as a postdoctoral researcher for several years.<ref name="Bjorken"/>

==Work==
Bjorken discovered in 1968 what is known as ''[[light-cone]] scaling'' (or '''''Bjorken scaling'''''), a phenomenon in the [[deep inelastic scattering]] of light on [[strong interaction|strongly interacting]] particles, known as ''[[hadron]]s'' (such as [[proton]]s and [[neutron]]s):
Experimentally observed hadrons behave as collections of virtually independent point-like constituents when probed at high energies.

Properties of these hadrons scale, that is, they are determined not by the absolute energy of an experiment, but, instead,  by dimensionless kinematic quantities, such as a scattering angle or the ratio of the energy to a momentum transfer. Because increasing energy implies potentially improved spatial resolution, scaling implies independence of the absolute resolution scale, and hence effectively point-like substructure.

This observation was critical to the recognition of [[quark]]s as actual [[elementary particle]]s (rather than just convenient theoretical constructs), and led to the theory of [[strong interaction]]s known as [[quantum chromodynamics]], where it was understood in terms of the [[asymptotic freedom]] property.   In Bjorken's picture, the quarks become point-like, observable objects at very short distances (high energies), shorter than the size of the hadrons.

Bjorken also discovered the '''''Bjorken [[Sum rules (Quantum Field Theory)|sum rule]]''''',<ref name="Bj. SR 1">[https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.148.1467 J. D. Bjorken (1966) “Applications of the chiral U(6)×U(6) algebra of current densities”] Phys. Rev. 148, 1467</ref><ref name="Bj. SR 2">[https://inspirehep.net/files/639d14249a23be3f8107142df1e6cd75 J. D. Bjorken (1970) “Inelastic scattering of polarized leptons from polarized nucleons”] Phys. Rev. D 1, 1376</ref> the prototypical QCD spin sum rule. It states that in the ''Bjorken scaling'' domain, the integral of the spin [[structure function]] of the [[proton]] minus that of the [[neutron]] is proportional to the [[axial current|axial charge]] of the [[nucleon]]. Specially: {{#tag:math|\int_0^1 dx (g_1^p(x)-g_1^n(x)) = g_A/6}}, where {{#tag:math|x}} is the Bjorken scaling variable, {{#tag:math|g_1^{p(n)}(x)}} is the first spin [[structure function]] of the proton (neutron), and {{#tag:math|g_A}} is the nucleon axial charge that characterizes the [[Free neutron decay|neutron β-decay]]. The sum rule was experimentally verified within better than a 10% precision.<ref name="SR review">[https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.05250 A. Deur, S. J. Brodsky, G. F. de Teramond (2019) “The Spin Structure of the Nucleon”] Rept. Prog. Phys. 82 076201</ref>

Bjorken was also among the first to point out the phenomena of [[jet quenching]] in heavy ion collisions in 1982.

[[Richard Feynman]] subsequently reformulated this concept into the [[parton (particle physics)|parton model]], used to understand the quark composition of hadrons at high energies.<ref>[http://www-zeus.desy.de/~liuc/physics/parton.pdf The Parton Model by P. Hansson, KTH, November 18, 2004] PDF file</ref> The predictions of Bjorken scaling were confirmed in the early late 1960s electroproduction experiments at [[SLAC]], in which quarks were seen for the first time.  The general idea, with small logarithmic modifications, is explained in quantum chromodynamics by "[[asymptotic freedom]]".

Bjorken co-authored, with [[Sidney Drell]], a classic companion volume textbook on [[relativistic quantum mechanics]] and [[quantum field]]s.

==Personal life and death==
In 1967, Bjorken married Joan Goldthwaite; they had two children and were married until her death in 1983.<ref name = Miller>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2024/08/30/science/james-bjorken-dead.html|title = James Bjorken, 90, Who Helped Discover Quarks|page = A20|last = Miller|first = Katrina|date = August 31, 2024|accessdate = August 31, 2024|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|url-access = limited}}</ref> He lived in [[Sky Londa, California]].<ref name = Miller/>

Bjorken died from [[melanoma]] at a care facility in [[Redwood City, California]], on August 6, 2024 at the age of 90.<ref name = Miller/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Remembering theoretical physicist James D. "BJ" Bjorken, 90, who played a crucial role in discovering quarks |url=https://www6.slac.stanford.edu/news/2024-08-14-remembering-theoretical-physicist-james-d-bj-bjorken-90-who-played-crucial-role |access-date=2024-08-15 |website=SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory |language=en}}</ref>
